meta.name: French Bulldog Puppy Checklist
meta.excerpt: What to have ready before your Frenchie comes home — including the insurance timing window most new owners miss, and what the first vet visit should address for a brachycephalic breed.
meta.meta_description: French Bulldog puppy checklist: supplies, first-week plan, insurance timing, and what to watch for at the first vet visit.

intro.label: Before They Arrive
intro.heading: What to Have Ready Before Your Frenchie Comes Home
intro.html:
French Bulldogs settle into new homes quickly — they're adaptable, sociable, and not prone to the acute anxiety some other breeds show in the first days. But there are a handful of breed-specific preparations that matter more for a Frenchie than generic puppy guides cover.

Two things above everything else: get pet insurance applied for before the first vet visit, and make sure your home is properly climate-controlled. These aren't optional considerations for a brachycephalic breed — they're the foundation the rest of ownership builds on.

care.label: The Full List
care.heading: Supplies Checklist
care.html:
Containment & Sleep

  • Medium crate with divider — medium is the right permanent size for an adult Frenchie (20–28 lbs); use the divider to make it smaller for housetraining
  • Soft washable dog bed — Frenchies are not heavy chewers; a decent bed lasts
  • Baby gate or X-pen — for managing the puppy's space during housetraining

Feeding

  • Stainless steel bowls (2) — small breed appropriate; avoid deep bowls that can cause the dog to strain their neck awkwardly
  • Small-breed puppy food — ask the breeder what they've been feeding; transition gradually over 7–10 days
  • Slow feeder bowl — Frenchies eat fast; slowing intake reduces air swallowing and digestive upset

Collar, Harness & ID

  • Harness (not collar) — important for brachycephalic breeds; collar pressure on the trachea adds to breathing difficulty; use a harness as the primary attachment point
  • 4–6 foot leash — standard for training
  • ID tag with your phone number — have this ready before pickup

Grooming

  • Unscented dog wipes or baby wipes — for daily wrinkle cleaning; start this from day one
  • Rubber grooming mitt or soft brush — for weekly coat brushing
  • Ear cleaner and cotton balls — for weekly ear checks
  • Nail clippers (small breed) — start handling paws from day one even if not trimming

Toys

  • Small Kong — for crate settling; fill with soft food or kibble
  • Rope toy (small) — for light tug play
  • Soft plush toy — Frenchies enjoy carrying soft toys

Health & Safety

  • Pet insurance — applied for before the first vet visit — the single most important item; BOAS and respiratory conditions noted at the first exam become pre-existing exclusions immediately
  • Air conditioning confirmed functional — non-negotiable for a brachycephalic breed in any warm climate
  • Vet appointment booked — within 3 days of arrival
  • Enzyme cleaner — for accident cleanup

special.label: First Week
special.heading: First Week Plan and What to Watch For
special.html:
Day 1–2: Calm Introduction

Frenchies are social and adjust to new environments reasonably well, but still benefit from quiet time to settle. Limit visitors in the first 48 hours. Start the crate routine from night one — consistency in the first week resolves nighttime whining faster than giving in does. Start wrinkle cleaning from day one, even briefly, so it becomes a normal part of the routine.

Day 3: First Vet Visit — What to Address

For a French Bulldog specifically, ask your vet to:

  • Assess the nostrils and airway — are they open enough to breathe comfortably? This is the BOAS baseline evaluation.
  • Check the soft palate — an elongated palate is the other common BOAS component; early identification matters
  • Discuss the vaccination schedule and when flea/tick/heartworm prevention should start
  • Baseline weight — Frenchies can become overweight quickly, and obesity worsens breathing

Watch for Heat and Breathing

In the first week, you'll learn what your Frenchie's baseline breathing sounds like. Some noise — snuffling, snoring, occasional snorts — is normal. Labored breathing at rest, open-mouth breathing, blue-tinged gums, or collapse are emergencies. Know the difference and know where your nearest emergency vet is.

The Most Common Mistake New Frenchie Owners Make

Delaying pet insurance. The reasoning is usually "I'll get it after the first vet visit" — but that's exactly when the window closes. Any condition, even a minor mention of noisy breathing or narrowed nostrils, becomes a pre-existing exclusion on day one of coverage. Apply before that first appointment. This is the piece of advice that matters most financially for French Bulldog owners.

faq.q: Should I use a harness or collar for a French Bulldog puppy?
faq.a: Harness, always. Pressure on the trachea from a collar adds to the airway restriction that brachycephalic breeds already have. A flat collar is fine for holding an ID tag, but leash attachment should always be to a properly fitted harness. This is one of the few breed-specific equipment choices that genuinely matters for health reasons, not just preference.

faq.q: My French Bulldog puppy snores loudly. Is this normal?
faq.a: Some snoring and snuffling is normal for the breed — the flat face creates narrower airways than most breeds have. Loud snoring at rest, snoring that's getting worse, or difficulty breathing during mild activity are reasons to talk to your vet sooner rather than later. A vet experienced with brachycephalic breeds can assess whether what you're hearing is within normal range or indicates early BOAS that would benefit from early intervention.

faq.q: How do I housetrain a French Bulldog puppy?
faq.a: Consistent schedule: out immediately after waking, after meals, and after play. Crate training helps — dogs don't like to soil their sleeping area, and a properly sized crate (small enough that there's no corner to eliminate in) supports housetraining significantly. Frenchies can take longer to housetrain than some breeds. Patience and consistency over 8–12 weeks is realistic. Clean accidents thoroughly with enzyme cleaner to remove scent markers.

faq.q: Can French Bulldog puppies go outside in summer?
faq.a: With precautions. Early morning (before 9am) or evening (after 7pm) only on warm days. No activity when ambient temperature exceeds 75°F (24°C) — even walking. Always carry water and watch for signs of overheating: excessive panting, drooling, slowing down, or collapsing. Keep walks short and never push through heat for the sake of exercise. A Frenchie that needs to stay inside on a hot day is better off inside.
